lines.text: What causes a reduction in pulmonary functional residual capacity?
Functional residual capacity is the air left in the lungs at the end of passive expiration. Here it is this little jar.
(sigh) These lungs have turned to wood. That is pulmonary fibrosis.
Fibrosis makes the lungs stiff and less compliant, like this tight spring.
Stiff lungs hold less air at rest, so the F R C is reduced.
Obstructive diseases, like emphysema, chronic bronchitis and asthma, do the opposite. Air trapping and higher compliance increase the F R C.
Remember: restrictive disease, like pulmonary fibrosis, reduces the functional residual capacity.
Which is a feature of the physiology of angiotensin two?
The answer is: released in hypovolaemia.
This water tank is almost empty and very thirsty. That is hypovolaemia, a low blood volume.
Low volume switches on the renin–angiotensin system. Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin one.
Angiotensin one is then converted into angiotensin two, our muscular hero.
(laugh) He squeezes the blood vessel hard. Angiotensin two is one of the most potent vasoconstrictors in the body.
Narrowing the vessels helps hold up blood pressure when the volume is low.
Remember: angiotensin two, the great squeezer, is released in hypovolaemia.
